section.title: My Help Comes from the Lord
section.sectionRationale: The second of the fifteen Songs of Ascents, Psalms 120 to 134, sung by pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, placed in Book V of the Psalter, Psalms 107 to 150. It answers the distress of Psalm 120 with a confident confession of the LORD as the pilgrim's tireless guardian on the road.
section.thesis: The LORD who made heaven and earth is an ever watchful keeper who never slumbers, sheltering His people from every danger by day and night, from this moment until forevermore.
section.frameNote: Two movements marked by a question and its answer: the question of where help comes from and the confession that it comes from the LORD, verses 1 to 2, and the sixfold declaration of His unsleeping keeping, verses 3 to 8.

units.label: My help comes from the Lord

verses.text: I lift up my eyes to the hills. From where does my help come?
My help comes from the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.

units.label: He who keeps you will not slumber

verses.text: He will not allow your foot to slip; your {{shomer|Protector}} will not slumber.
Behold, the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep.
The LORD is your keeper; the LORD is the shade on your right hand.
The sun will not strike you by day, nor the moon by night.
The LORD will guard you from all evil; He will preserve your {{nephesh|soul}}.
The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore.

shomer.gloss: Keeper, guardian, watchman. The same root, shamar, is repeated six times across this short psalm, forming its backbone: the LORD is the tireless watchman who never dozes off duty.

nephesh.gloss: Soul, life, the whole self. The LORD's keeping reaches beyond the physical journey to preserve the pilgrim's very life and being.

basic.context: This Song of Ascents pictures a pilgrim scanning the hills along the road to Jerusalem, hills that could hide bandits as easily as offer help, and answering his own question: help comes not from the hills but from the LORD who made them.
basic.hermeneutics: It describes the specific comfort of pilgrims facing real dangers on the road, sun, moon, slipping feet, and it prescribes as an abiding pattern trusting the LORD's unsleeping care rather than the created world itself.
basic.originalLanguages: The Hebrew root shamar, keep or guard, is repeated six times, forming a drumbeat of assurance. The LORD's keeping reaches to the nephesh, the whole soul and life, not merely the body on the road.
basic.typology: The LORD's tireless watch, who neither slumbers nor sleeps, anticipates Christ, who though He slept in the boat in His humanity, awoke to command the wind and waves with the same divine authority this psalm ascribes to God alone.
basic.christ: Jesus is the good shepherd who never slumbers over His sheep, John 10:28 to 29, and He is Immanuel, God with us, whose keeping power is not confined to a single road or a single lifetime but reaches to eternal life.
basic.god: God is the Maker of heaven and earth who personally keeps His people, unsleeping, unshaded from His care by day or by night, guarding both body and soul from this moment forever.
basic.crossReferences: John 10:28-29 shows Jesus keeping His sheep so that none can be snatched away. Mark 4:38-39 shows Jesus, though asleep in the boat, awaking with full authority over the storm. Jude 24-25 praises the One able to keep believers from stumbling.
basic.oneStory: This psalm's confession that help comes only from the Maker of heaven and earth runs forward to Christ, in whom that same unsleeping, all sufficient keeping is given fully and finally to His people.

context.literary:
Psalm 121 has two halves with a change of voice between them. In verses 1 and 2 a single speaker says 'I' and 'my,' asks a question and answers it. From verse 3 the speaker is addressed as 'you,' and the voice that speaks is not the one that asked. The pilgrim's private question is answered by a second voice, perhaps a priest, a companion or his own heart reminding him, and the rest of the poem is that answer, eight verses of promise.

The poem is built on one root. The keeper is named in verses 3, 4, 5, 7 and 8, and each time the verb or noun is shamar, six times in all, as the lexicon notes, so that a hearer of the Hebrew is surrounded by the sound. The name of the LORD appears five times, in verses 2, 5, 7 and 8, and the keeper is the LORD each time. It is the repetition of a lullaby, and it is meant to be calming.

The movement of the promise is a widening of range. It begins with the foot, which is the smallest and most immediate point of danger, verse 3. It goes on to the whole day and night, the sun and the moon, verse 6, then to all evil and the soul, verse 7, and finally to every coming and going, now and for ever, verse 8. The psalm starts at the pilgrim's feet and ends at the horizon of time.

The poem is also a series of contrasts. The pilgrim looks up at the hills and the LORD made the hills. The pilgrim's foot may slip and the keeper does not sleep. The sun by day and the moon by night are paired as opposites that together cover all the hours. The poem is bound by these pairs: day and night, going out and coming in, now and for ever.
context.historical:
The road to Jerusalem is uphill from almost every direction. From Jericho it climbs more than three thousand feet in a short distance through barren, rocky country, and Jesus' parable of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, Luke 10:30, shows how dangerous that road could be. A pilgrim on foot faced uneven paths, loose stones, bandits in the rocks and a fierce sun for most of the day, and he might sleep out under the open sky at night.

The hills of verse 1 therefore carried more than one meaning. They were the way to Jerusalem, set high among the mountains, for 'As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people,' Psalm 125:2. Zion itself was spoken of with mountain imagery, Psalm 48:1 to 2 and Psalm 87:1. But the hills were also where the people of the land set their shrines on high places, and where thieves hid. A pilgrim who lifts his eyes is looking at what he must climb and at what might harm him, and he is also looking for the first sight of the goal.

The promises of verses 5 and 6 reflect real hazards of travel in Palestine. The sun beat on a person walking in the open, and the 'shade' on the right hand pictures a protector who stands on the side of the sword arm, the defender's place, as in Psalm 16:8 and Psalm 109:31. The moon by night is less certain, since interpreters differ on what harm is meant, whether cold, fear or the superstitions of the nations, and the psalm's point does not depend on settling it.

The phrase 'your coming and going' in verse 8 is the language of daily life and work, as in Deuteronomy 28:6, 'You will be blessed when you come in and blessed when you go out.' It covers the leaving of the house for the road and the return afterward.
context.canonical:
The psalm has close companions. Psalm 124:8 says, 'Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth,' almost the words of Psalm 121:2, and Psalm 134:3 ends the whole collection with 'May the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.' The pilgrims begin and end with the same creator.

The verb of keeping is the verb of the priestly blessing. 'May the LORD bless you and keep you,' Numbers 6:24, uses the same root, and Psalm 121 reads like a long unfolding of that line. It is also the verb of God's word to Jacob, 'I am with you, and I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land,' Genesis 28:15. Jacob was leaving the land under promise when he heard it, and this psalm applies his promise to every Israelite who travels.

The image of the shade is used widely. Isaiah 25:4 calls the LORD 'a shade from the heat,' Psalm 91:1 speaks of the shadow of the Almighty, and Numbers 14:9 says the protection of the Canaanites has been removed. Isaiah 49:10 says that for the redeemed no scorching heat or sun will beat down on them, and Revelation 7:16 takes up the same words for the multitude before the throne.

The unsleeping God is set against Elijah's mockery of the prophets of Baal, 'Perhaps he is sleeping and must be awakened!' 1 Kings 18:27, and against the cries of the afflicted who say 'Wake up, O Lord! Why are You sleeping?' Psalm 44:23. The New Testament uses the psalm's confidence for believers: Jude 24 praises him who is able to keep them from stumbling, 1 Peter 1:5 says they are 'shielded by God's power,' and Jesus prays that the Father will keep His own from the evil one, John 17:15.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer set out to reassure travellers, and he does it by changing the subject of the journey. The pilgrim's attention is on the road, the hills and the heat. The psalm turns it to the one who is keeping watch over the road. The question in verse 1 is honest, since the road is dangerous, and the answer is not 'nothing will happen' but 'the keeper does not sleep.'

He also wanted the pilgrims to hear a promise that was personal. The 'you' that runs through verses 3 to 8 is singular in Hebrew, so each pilgrim in the crowd is addressed by himself. The Israel of verse 4 is the community, but the foot, the shade and the soul are those of one man, so a person can hear the psalm as spoken to him.

And he meant the psalm to cure a particular fear, that of being alone and unseen on a hard road. The God who made the heavens and the earth has not left the pilgrim to his own strength, and the pilgrim who arrives at Jerusalem does not owe his arrival to his own cleverness. The proper response is to thank the keeper at the end of the journey, which is how the next psalm begins, 'I was glad when they said to me, Let us go to the house of the LORD,' Psalm 122:1.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records a promise of protection, and it should be read as a statement of God's care and not as a guarantee that nothing bad will happen to a believer on any road. Believers have been robbed, burned and killed on their journeys. Jesus told His followers that some of them would be put to death, and in the same breath promised that 'not even a hair of your head will perish,' Luke 21:16 to 18. The two statements stand together, and they show that 'all evil' in verse 7 is about final safety of the soul and the person, which the next phrase makes plain, 'He will preserve your soul.'

It would also be a misreading to turn the psalm into a reason to be careless. The pilgrims did not leave their staffs, their food or their companions at home. Faith in the keeper is not an excuse for foolishness, as Jesus said to the devil who quoted another psalm about angels, Matthew 4:6 to 7.

What the psalm prescribes is a settled trust and the habit of looking up. It teaches believers to ask the right question about their help, and to answer it by the Creator's name. The promise belongs to those who belong to the LORD, and it assures them that no stage of their life is outside his care.

debates.question: Does lifting the eyes to the hills in verse 1 express hope or apprehension?

views.label: The hills represent hope, since Jerusalem and the temple sit on high ground
views.case: Pilgrims literally looked toward the hills of Zion as their destination and source of worship, so the gaze is naturally hopeful.

views.label: The hills represent danger, since bandits and pagan high places lurked there
views.case: The question that follows, 'From where does my help come', reads more naturally as genuine uncertainty answered by turning away from the hills themselves to the LORD who made them.

debates.bearing: Either reading reaches the same conclusion: the psalmist's confidence rests not in the hills as such but in the LORD who made heaven and earth.

debates.question: Who is speaking in verses 3 to 8?

views.label: A priest or companion answering the pilgrim
views.case: The shift from 'I' to 'you' after verse 2 suggests a second speaker, and the language of keeping resembles the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24. It may reflect a liturgy in which pilgrims were sent on their way with a blessing.

views.label: The pilgrim, preaching to himself
views.case: Psalms often have a speaker address his own soul, as in Psalm 42:5. The sudden 'you' could be the pilgrim reminding himself of what he believes.

views.label: The pilgrim in verses 1 and 2, and God himself in the rest
views.case: Some hear the voice of the LORD answering in the second half, since the promises are in the first person of a keeper. The text, however, speaks of the LORD in the third person throughout, which makes this the least natural reading.

debates.bearing: The doctrine is unaffected. Whether the voice is a priest's, a friend's or his own, the promise is the LORD's and is spoken to one who has just confessed his need.

debates.question: Is 'will not allow your foot to slip' a promise or a prayer?

views.label: A confident promise
views.case: The BSB reads the verb as a future assurance, and the surrounding verses use plain statements of fact, 'The sun will not strike you.' The psalm is meant to settle the pilgrim's anxiety.

views.label: A wish or blessing
views.case: The negative in the Hebrew of verse 3 is the form often used for wishes, 'May He not let your foot slip,' as in a blessing. The whole psalm would then be a prayer on behalf of the pilgrim.

debates.bearing: The difference is small. A blessing spoken in the name of the LORD is a promise that rests on his character, and a promise that is spoken is received as a blessing.

study.originalLanguages:
The question in verse 1 is 'From where does my help come?' and the word for help is ezer, a word with a lofty record. It is what God makes for Adam in a 'suitable helper,' Genesis 2:18, and it is the word Moses uses when he names his son because 'The God of my father was my helper,' Exodus 18:4. Deuteronomy 33:29 calls the LORD 'the shield that protects you,' using the same family of words, and Psalm 33:20 says 'He is our help and our shield.' To call for ezer is to call for someone who comes alongside with strength, and not for an inferior or an aid.

The verb of the psalm is shamar, to keep, guard, watch. It means to post a guard and to pay attention to what one guards, and the noun shomer, as in verses 3 to 5, is the watchman at the city gate or the shepherd who keeps the flock. The same verb is used for guarding the garden in Genesis 2:15, and for the priestly blessing in Numbers 6:24. A keeper is someone who has a charge to hold, and the psalm announces that the LORD has taken the pilgrim as his charge.

Verse 3 has the negative 'al' with the verb, 'may he not give your foot to totter,' where the verb for slipping is mot, to shake or give way, as in Psalm 66:9, 'keeps our feet from slipping,' and Psalm 37:24, 'Though he falls, he will not be overwhelmed.' The verb is used of a foot on uneven ground, and the picture is of a loose stone on a mountain path.

The pair 'slumber' and 'sleep' in verses 3 and 4 are two words, yanum and yishan, the lighter and the deeper kind of rest. The poem says the keeper does neither, so there is no state of drowsiness in which he can be caught out. The 'Behold' that opens verse 4 asks the hearer to look again at what has just been said, and the emphasis is on the title 'Keeper of Israel,' shomer Yisrael, which gathers the individual under the people.

The 'shade' in verse 5 is tsel, the word for a covering from the sun and for the protection of a nearer person. The phrase 'on your right hand' is a place, the side of the defender, as in Psalm 16:8. The LORD is not only above the pilgrim but at his side.

Verse 7 ends with the nephesh, the 'soul,' the whole living person. And verse 8 closes with the pairing 'your going out and your coming in,' tse'tekha uvo'ekha, a phrase that sums up all of life's activity, followed by the opening of time, 'from now and unto the age,' me'attah ve'ad olam, rendered 'both now and forevermore.' It is the same phrase that closes Psalm 125:2.

typology.type: The pilgrim's ascent to Jerusalem, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: The pilgrim lifts his eyes to the hills that lead to Zion and is kept on the road. Jesus makes the same ascent as the one who 'resolutely set out for Jerusalem,' Luke 9:51, and what He does there makes the city a place that believers can reach. Hebrews tells them 'you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem,' Hebrews 12:22, with Jesus the mediator, Hebrews 12:24. The correspondence is that the journey ends at God's city. The type falls short because the pilgrims climbed to an earthly city and had to go home again, whereas believers come to a Zion they never leave.

typology.type: The keeper who does not sleep, verses 3 to 4
typology.fulfillment: The LORD's vigilance is stated in absolute terms, and the Gospels place beside it an image that startles: Jesus asleep in the stern of the boat while the storm rages, Mark 4:38. The disciples woke Him, and He rebuked the wind and the sea, Mark 4:39, doing what the psalms ascribe to the LORD, as in Psalm 107:28 to 29 and Psalm 89:9. The correspondence is not that Jesus slept in the same way the psalm denies, but that the one who rests as a man rules as God. The type falls short because the sleeping was part of Christ's real humanity, and it points out that His authority was not suspended while he slept.

typology.type: The shepherd keeper and his sheep, verses 5 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The keeper who guards the soul from all evil is the shepherd of Israel, Psalm 80:1 and Psalm 100:3. Jesus claims the role: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and He says that none of His sheep will be snatched from His hand or from the Father's, John 10:28 to 29. In John 17:12 He tells the Father that while He was with them He protected and preserved them. The correspondence is that the keeping is now personal and costly. The type falls short because the psalm's keeper watches without a price, while Jesus keeps His sheep by giving His life for them.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ through its central claim, that the keeper of his people is the LORD himself. When the Gospels show Jesus doing the keeper's work, they are showing who he is. The good shepherd who lays down his life, John 10:11, is the shepherd of Psalm 80:1 and Psalm 100:3, and when he says 'No one can snatch them out of My hand,' and then speaks of the Father's hand in the same breath, John 10:28 to 29, the double assurance is the 'keeper of Israel' of verse 4, shared by the Son and the Father.

It leads to Christ in the storm scene. The disciples wake the sleeping Jesus with an accusation, 'don't You care that we are perishing?' Mark 4:38. He rebukes the wind and sea, and they ask, 'Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?' Mark 4:41. The answer is in the psalms: it is the LORD who rules the raging sea, Psalm 89:9, and who calms the storm to a whisper, Psalm 107:29. The God who never slumbers and the man who sleeps in the boat are one Lord, and the details of the scene guard both truths. A reader should not claim the psalm predicted this episode; the point is that the Gospel accounts treat Jesus as the one to whom the psalm's title belongs.

It leads to Christ in his prayer. On the night he was betrayed, Jesus asked the Father to keep his own, 'I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one,' John 17:15, and he said that he had protected and preserved them by the Father's name, John 17:12. That is verse 7, 'The LORD will guard you from all evil,' spoken by the Son as a request and answered by the Father. Jesus' own promise at the end of Matthew, 'I am with you always, even to the end of the age,' Matthew 28:20, is the 'forevermore' of verse 8 as a person's word.

It leads to Christ by the shape of the journey. Jesus goes up to Jerusalem Himself, Luke 9:51, and the keeping that the psalm promised to the pilgrim He fulfils for his people by passing through what the pilgrim feared. Hebrews says believers are kept by God's power, 1 Peter 1:5, and that He is 'able to keep you from stumbling,' Jude 24. The keeper who seemed to ask the pilgrim to look up has himself come down to the road.

One caution: the hills, the sun and the moon are not coded pictures of Christ's person. The links above rest on the New Testament's own claims about who keeps and shepherds God's people, and on how the Gospels present Jesus.
study.god:
This is the psalm's whole theology in one sentence: the one who made heaven and earth is the one who keeps the pilgrim's foot. The Creator is named at the very start, verse 2, and he is the same person as the keeper in verse 3 and the guard in verse 7. Power and care are not divided. The God whom the hills, which the pilgrim fears, owe their existence to is the one who is on the side of the traveller. Compare Psalm 90:1 to 2, where the God who is the dwelling place of his people is also the one who is God before the mountains were born.

He is wakeful. Other gods slept or were thought to, and Elijah's taunt in 1 Kings 18:27 is aimed at that idea. The psalm denies it for the LORD with two words, slumber and sleep, so that there is no shift in which his people are unwatched. Isaiah 40:28 says the same, that he 'will not grow tired or weary.' This is a statement about God's constancy, and it is also a quiet answer to the believer who has cried 'Wake up, O Lord!' as in Psalm 44:23. The cry is a sign of how it feels, and the psalm is a statement of how it is.

He is personal. The covenant name appears five times, and the keeper is described by three images of nearness: the one at the right hand, the shade over the head and the guard over the soul. There is no distance in this picture. He is also over Israel, the 'keeper of Israel,' verse 4, and so his care for the individual is part of his faithfulness to the covenant people.

He holds two truths together. The promise is 'all evil,' and yet believers meet evil. Paul asks whether trouble, distress, persecution or sword can separate us from the love of Christ and answers that none can, Romans 8:35 to 39. Jesus says some will be killed, and yet not a hair of their head will perish, Luke 21:16 to 18. The psalm does not settle this by denying suffering; it says that no harm reaches the soul, and the person, outside the keeper's hand, and that the keeping is not for a single stretch of the road but 'both now and forevermore,' verse 8. Protection here is a matter of final safety and not of a trouble-free road.

For worship, the psalm gives a way to begin each journey, each day and each night, by lifting the eyes and asking where help comes from, and then by answering with a name. It teaches a quiet confidence that lets a person sleep, because the one who does not sleep is on watch. Psalm 127:2 says that he gives sleep to his beloved, and Psalm 4:8 and Psalm 3:5 are the prayers of those who lie down in peace for that reason.

crossReferences.note: 'Our help is in the name of the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth' is nearly a repeat of Psalm 121:2, but in the plural. It shows the pilgrims taking the confession of one man and making it the confession of the whole company.

'As the mountains surround Jerusalem, so the LORD surrounds His people, both now and forevermore.' The hills that worried the pilgrim in Psalm 121:1 become a picture of God's protection, and the closing words match verse 8 of this psalm.

The priestly blessing begins 'May the LORD bless you and keep you,' using the same verb as Psalm 121. The psalm reads like an extended blessing in which the keeping promised in the benediction is described in detail.

God tells Jacob, who is leaving the land on a journey, 'I will watch over you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land.' This is the older form of the promise in Psalm 121, using the same verb, and it ties the pilgrim's safe going and returning to the covenant with Abraham's family.

Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal by suggesting their god may be sleeping and must be awakened. It is the sharpest contrast to Psalm 121:4, in which the LORD of Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps, and it shows what the psalm is denying.

The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth, who does not grow tired or weary. It supplies the reason behind Psalm 121:4: the keeper is the Creator, and the Creator does not tire.

For the redeemed, neither scorching heat nor sun will beat down on them. It carries the promise of Psalm 121:6 into the age of restoration, as God's compassionate guide leads his people to springs of water.

Jesus warns that some will be put to death and then says 'not even a hair of your head will perish.' It shows how the promise of keeping from all evil in Psalm 121:7 is to be read, as a promise about the person God preserves, and not a promise of a safe road.

Jesus says that His sheep will never perish and no one can snatch them from His hand or from His Father's hand. It is the Gospel answer to the psalm's keeper, with the keeping given both to the Son and to the Father.
Jesus asleep in the stern is woken and rebukes the wind and sea. The one who is a man at rest is also the Lord who governs the storm, which is the psalm's keeper seen in Jesus.

Believers are 'shielded by God's power' for a salvation to be revealed. The word shielded is a word for a garrison keeping watch, and it applies the psalm's keeping to the Christian's whole life until the end.
The doxology praises him who is able to keep believers from stumbling and to present them unblemished, which is the New Testament form of Psalm 121:3 and of the guarding of the soul in verse 7.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers one of the oldest questions of the Bible: where does a person's help come from? In the garden the man and woman were told to keep the garden, Genesis 2:15, and they were driven out of it, and cherubim were set to guard the way back, Genesis 3:24. Since then humanity has been outside, travelling. The question of the pilgrim in verse 1 is the question of the exiled race.

The Old Testament's answer is the promise to Jacob, the wandering heir of the promise, 'I will watch over you wherever you go,' Genesis 28:15, and the promise is made good for Israel in the exodus, where the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, Exodus 13:21 to 22. The cloud was a shade by day and a light by night, and Psalm 121:5 to 6 remembers it. The people who were kept in the wilderness are kept again on the pilgrim road.

The psalm sits on the long road between the exile and the return, and its comfort was needed on both. It also looks beyond the hills of Judah. The Songs of Ascents climb to the house of the LORD, but the prophets promise a time when the sun will no longer strike God's people, Isaiah 49:10, and the book of Revelation says it will be so, Revelation 7:16.

The story turns on Jesus. He is the shepherd who keeps his flock by giving his life, John 10:11, who stills the storm, Mark 4:39, who prays the Father will keep His own from the evil one, John 17:15, and who promises to be with them always, Matthew 28:20. The keeping that Israel's pilgrims asked for is given to a worldwide people, who are told they have come to Mount Zion, Hebrews 12:22.

And it ends in the new creation. There the journey is finished and the pilgrim is home, and the dangers of the road are gone. The sun does not beat down on them, Revelation 7:16, there is no more night, and the Lord God himself gives light, Revelation 22:5. The keeper's promise, 'both now and forevermore,' is fulfilled in the one place where it can be kept in full, in a city where God dwells with his people and wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:3 to 4.

sermon.title: My Help Comes from the Lord
sermon.why: Begg preaches this psalm directly by name, walking through its picture of the LORD as the pilgrim's tireless keeper and drawing out the assurance this gives for facing daily dangers with confidence in God's unsleeping care.

quiz.q: Where does the psalmist say his help ultimately comes from?

options.text: From the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth.
options.note: Verse 2 gives this direct answer to the question of verse 1.

options.text: From the hills themselves.
options.note: The hills prompt the question, but the answer redirects to the LORD who made them.

options.text: From his own strength and preparation.
options.note: The psalm explicitly locates help outside the psalmist, in the LORD.

options.text: From the watchmen on the city walls.
options.note: Watchmen appear elsewhere, such as Psalm 130, but here help comes from the LORD directly.

quiz.q: What is repeated to describe the LORD's care throughout this psalm?

options.text: That He keeps or guards His people, using the Hebrew root shamar six times.
options.note: This repetition forms the psalm's structural backbone.

options.text: That He forgives sin repeatedly.
options.note: Forgiveness is the theme of Psalm 130, not the keeping language here.

options.text: That He rebuilds the temple.
options.note: Temple building is not this psalm's subject.

options.text: That He blesses the harvest.
options.note: Harvest blessing appears in psalms like 126 and 128, not centrally here.

quiz.q: What does verse 4 emphasize about the LORD's watchfulness?

options.text: He will neither slumber nor sleep.
options.note: This is stated directly, intensifying verse 3's claim.

options.text: He rests on the Sabbath from watching.
options.note: The text specifically denies any slumber or sleep, even for rest.

options.text: He watches only during the day.
options.note: Verse 6 specifically extends His care to nighttime as well.

options.text: He watches only over kings.
options.note: The psalm says He watches over Israel broadly, not kings alone.

quiz.q: How far does the LORD's promised keeping extend, according to verse 8?

options.text: Over every coming and going, from this time forth and forevermore.
options.note: Verse 8 gives this comprehensive, eternal scope.

options.text: Only for the duration of one pilgrimage.
options.note: The psalm's language is deliberately unlimited, not tied to a single journey.

options.text: Only until the pilgrim reaches Jerusalem.
options.note: The promise is not bounded by arrival at a destination.

options.text: Only during the pilgrim's youth.
options.note: The text specifies forevermore, not a limited season of life.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's unsleeping Protector connect to Christ in the Gospels?

options.text: Jesus, though asleep in the boat, awoke to command the storm with the same divine authority this psalm gives to God alone.
options.note: Mark 4:38-39 shows Jesus exercising this very authority over creation.

options.text: It has no connection to the New Testament.
options.note: The Gospels directly echo this psalm's language of divine authority over storms and keeping.

options.text: It shows Jesus needing rescue from danger Himself.
options.note: The Gospel account shows Jesus as the one who calms danger, not one needing rescue.

options.text: It predicts the exact number of Jesus' miracles.
options.note: The connection is one of shared divine authority and pattern, not a numerical prediction.

questions: The psalmist lifts his eyes to the hills and then answers his own question by turning to the LORD. Where are you tempted to look for help in places that cannot ultimately give it?
Six times this psalm says the LORD keeps His people. Which specific situation in your life right now most needs to be entrusted to His unsleeping care?
The LORD is described as a shade against the sun and a guard against the moon. What fears, day or night, do you need to bring to Him as your shelter?
Jesus, though asleep in the boat, awoke with full authority over the storm. How does knowing Christ holds this same unsleeping power change how you face today's uncertainty?
The promise reaches from now to forevermore. How does trusting God's care for your whole life, not just this season, change the way you pray about your future?

translationNotes.note: The question 'From where does my help come' can be read as either hopeful anticipation of Zion or genuine uncertainty about danger in the hills; either way the answer that follows locates help in the LORD alone.
Protector renders shomer, keeper or guardian, from the root shamar which recurs six times across the psalm and forms its central theme.
Ancient belief associated both sunstroke and a form of moon related affliction with travel; the psalm answers both fears with the LORD's comprehensive, round the clock protection.
